carson-hardy-shell-creek-1900-08-21.A1:
Foul Play Suspected.
The body of an unknown negro was found last Tuesday near Shell Creek on the E. T. & W. N. C. railroad. There were thirty or more bullet holes in the corpse. This is supposed to be the negro, Carson Hardy, who was arrested for being drunk at Shell Creek and who later made some threats against his prosecutors. A barn was burned a few nights later and Hardy was arrested on suspicion. While in charge of the office he was shot to death.

henry-atkins-blythe-1900-07-28.A1:
Officers Outwitted the Mob.
Friday afternoon Henry Atkins, a negro, charged with assaulting and robbing Mr. F. E. Tinsley, a merchant at Blythe station in Richmond county, about a month ago, was arrested by Sheriff Ivey, of Glascock county, at Boyd's tie camp in the eastern portion of the county and brought to Gibson Friday night and lodged in jail Saturday morning. Sheriff Ivey, with his prisoner, accompanied by Colonel E. J. Hawkins, who was employed by the negro to represent him, boarded the early train, trying to turn him over to the Richmond county authorities, but arriving at Blythe they were met by a mob who were determined to lynch him. His life was saved only by the strategy of Messrs. Hawkins and Ivey, outwitting the mob by jumping aboard the east-bound train, which arrived in the nick of time.

jim-strickland-1900-08-18.A1:
Flogged For Threatening Whites.
(By the Associated Press.)
Griffin, Ga., Ang. 18.—Jim Strickland, a negro living in Henry county, was taken out by a crowd and given 150 lashes on the bare back and then shot once in the arm, twice in the thigh and once in the leg.

Stirckland has been using highly incendiary talk, saying what he would do if a white man crossed his path and has been regarded as a fire-brand in the community. He had been repeatedly warned to modify his language and actions, but these warnings had no effect. The mob went about its work quietly but effectively. After they had finished with the unfortunate wretch, he was taken to the house of a negro and his injuries attended to. It is not thought that he will die.

meridian-meridian-1900-08.A1:
STATE NEWS.
Columbus will have a paid fire department.
The hay crop is the best in Mississippi for years.
West Point is making efforts for a handsome union depot.
Magnolia gave 10 1-16 cents for her first bale and a barrel of flour.
The Deaf and Dumb Institute will open on the first Wednesday in October.
Centreville needs more residences and wants a Building and Loan Association.

smithfield-smithfield-1900-07-31.A1:
RUN OUT BY RED SHIRTS. VIOLENCE IN NORTH CAROLINA'S CAMPAIGN AT SMITHFIELD. Senator Butler's Substitute Taken From a Platform and Ordered From the Place-No Delay in Going—Republican Editor Threatened and Gov. Russell Orders Out Militia Order Countermanded a Little Afterward.
RALEIGH, N. C., July 31.—The first conflict during the present heated campaign occurred to-day at Smithfield, a small town thirty miles from here. Gov. Russell to-night ordered out the Raleigh light infantry to go to the scene of the trouble. The company had boarded a military special and was about to move out of the Union station, where thousands of people had congregated when the order for the movement was cancelled.

Gov. Russell had decided to send the troops upon the application of J. D. Parker, a Republican, who edits the Smithfield Courier, a country weekly. Parker telegraphed the Governor that a mob of red shirts and others had surrounded his office, that they were threatening to destroy the building and his plant, and that his life was in danger. Two appeals came to the Governor from Parker.

Just as the military special with the Light Infantry aboard was preparing to leave the Governor received a telegram from Sheriff Ellington saying that there was no necessity for troops and that the people did not want them. He said that he could protect life and property. The Governor then gave orders for the return of the company to the armory, where it is on duty waiting to be called if needed. The company will remain at the armory throughout the night.

The trouble started at Smithfield at noon. Senator Butler had an engagement to speak there, but he sent N. M. Teague in his place. Smithfield is a Democratic stronghold, and a big rally had been arranged. There were 5,000 persons present many of them wearing red shirts and carrying rifles. When Teague started to speak the Red Shirts gathered around him and pulled the platform upon which he was standing from under him. They gave him five minutes to get out of the town and he took the first road. Some of the friends of the Populist campaigners attempted to shove the Red Shirts aside when Teague was pulled down and this precipitated a general fight. Sticks were used and two persons were cut.

The Red Shirts ran the belligerent Populist out of sight. A solitary negro in the crowd was handled roughly. After disposing of the Populists the Red Shirts returned and heard their speakers out.

Later in the afternoon the demonstration was made against Editor Parker. He locked himself up in the second story of his building. Wise heads induced the crowd to disperse. There is bitter feeling against Parker. Further trouble is expected to-night.

The Legislature adjourned sine die this afternoon, it being the belief of leading Democrats that it is too late for the fusion leaders to interfere with the election on Thursday.

WILMINGTON, N. C., July 31.—Wilmington and New Hanover county campaign managers are rather resting to-night confident of a sweeping victory on the anti-negro amendment and for the Democratic ticket on Thursday, when the franchise amendment and general State and county elections will be held. The last demonstration of the campaign hereabouts was that to-night, during which speeches were made by John D. Bellamy, member of Congress for the Sixth district and Col. A. M. Waddell, who led the 1898 revolution in Wilmington overthrowing the fusion-negro regime, which was then in the saddle. No especially notable demonstration amended the speaking. Probably 1,000 persons attended.

No Red Shirts or firearms were visible. The fact is there is practically no opposition in Wilmington or the county to the amendment and campaign ticket. Not more than thirty-five negroes will vote in the county. Sixty-five negroes registered in Castle Hayne township were challenged, and failing to appear and show cause why they should not be debarred from voting will not be allowed to cast ballots on Thursday. All of them would have voted against the amendment. It is conceded that Columbus, Pender, Duplin, Onslow, Bladen, and other southeastern counties will give large majorities for the amendment. Brunswick, the most doubtful county in this region, it is thought will go for the amendment by a small majority.

There is still considerable apprehension that some scheme will be sprung by Butler to block the election on Thursday. Especially does this fear exist in the middle part of the State. The joint discussion at Clinton, Sampson county, to-day between Rudolph Duffy (Dem.) and ex-Congressman J. E. Fowler (Pop.), regarding which there was much apprehension of trouble, passed over very quietly. Only twelve Red Shirts attended. The crowd consisted of 600 negroes, 300 Populists and 200 Democrats. Red Shirts were restrained by campaign managers from attending in order that the possibility of trouble might be avoided. The estimate of a victory for the amendment by from 40,000 to 50,000 is still adhered to by campaign leaders of the opposition.
smithfield-smithfield-1900-07-31.A2:
NOT CALLED BY SHERIFF
Hon. Ed. W. Pou Made a Splendid Speech and Was Interrupted.
BUTLER WAS BURNED IN EFFIGY
The Men Who Interrupted Pou Cursed and Swore in the Presence of Ladies and a Small Panic Was Started. They Tried to Break Up Meeting.
(Special to News and Observer.)

Smithfield, N. C., July 31.—Hon. E. W. Pou spoke today on his native heath to five thousand men and ladies. The speech occurred in a large warehouse. Butler or Thompson were expected to divide time. Neither came, but Pou was interrupted in the midst of his speech with an announcement that a man by the name of Teague was present to divide time. Pou refused the substitute. It was known that Pou was hurrying to make the train to reach his next appointment and this was a concerted plan to create trouble. Three or four Republicans arose and began to curse and use profane language, shaking their fists greatly to consternation of the ladies, and a panic seemed imminent. The men were seized and hustled unceremoniously out of the house, but Pou spoke right on and avoided panic. The men could be heard outside swearing they would break up the meeting.

They broke into court house and began to ring the bell. Pou said, "Pay no attention to them. Listen to me." The audience obeyed, but the Republicans put Teague on a box outside of the court house and he began to lambaste Democrats in the most exasperating terms. It looked then as though there might be trouble but a few determined red shirts walked over and took Teague down and told him to "Git" and he "Got," as did also the others. Pou finished his speech without other interruption. He called upon all in favor of the amendment to rise, and everybody arose.

Space forbids a description of the parade. It was the most handsome and elaborate affair ever seen at a political gathering here.

After the speaking, a comic parade was instituted. Heading the procession was a red shirt, carrying a large cage containing a white rooster. Following him came four red shirts bearing above their heads a coffin with FUSION in large letters on each side, in which they announced reposed the remains of "Judas Iscariot Butler." Behind them came the band solemnly keeping step to muffled drums. A crowd of five hundred followed with shouts of laughter. They marched around the square and halted in front of the court house, while the band played a solemn dirge. They gently lowered the coffin, poured oil on it and touched the match. The band then struck up Dixie. Red shirts joined hands around the funeral pile and as the flames sprang heavenward danced around, keeping time to music.

This grotesque orgie ended the exercises of the day. One or two thoughtless cried out, "Let's go and tear the type out of the Courier office." Sheriff Ellington, who sat in the hotel piazza looking benignly on, walked over to the crowd and said, "Come, come boys, we can't have anything like that. ou have done enough now. This thing must stop right here." The crowd disavowed any intention of allowing such a thing to be done. But word reached J. D. Parker, the editor, and he affected terrible fright, especially when one H. M. Barnes, a Republican revenue doodle, walked into his office and laid two pistols on his table, swearing he had come to die with him in the protection of his property and that he would kill the Democrats. He swore he would get even with them for today's work on the night after election if not before. Sheriff Ellington hearing that Parker was greatly agitated went to Parker's office and told him that he should have the full protection of his office if it cost the last drop of his blood, and that nobody was going to harm his property, and had no serious intention of doing so. Every one supposed that the matter had ended there and the crowd dispersed to their homes, leaving almost no one in town not living here, but Parker wishing to make political capital, true to his Republican nature, sent a telegram to Governor Russell to send troops to suppress a riot. Later it was learned that a train was being prepared and troops coming from Raleigh. Everybody hooted the idea. Then came a 'phone message from Selma that the Coast Line crew and engine were in readiness.

Sheriff Ellington then sent the following message: "Hon. D. L. Russell, I have been informed that J. D. Parker, editor of the Smithfield Courier, has applied to you for troops to protect his property. There is no cause for any such request. There is no disturbance in town and but few men in town who do not live here.

(Signed) "J. T. ELLINGTON,
"Sheriff Johnston County."

Everything is quiet in town.

H. A. CHAPPELL.
smithfield-smithfield-1900-07-31.A4:
THE SMITHFIELD AND DUNN OUTRAGE.
The Democratic Redshirts tried to break up a Populist speaking. Blood shed followed. The Governor's Guard were ordered out to protect life, liberty and property. Mr. J. D. Parker, of Smithfield, was in Raleigh the other day and gave THE CAUCASIAN the following statement:

"A speaking had been appointed by the Populists for Smithfield on July 31st. After this was done, the democrats also appointed that day for speaking. The red shirts came into the township and the Democrats assembled at the Riverside Warehouse, where E. W. Pou, the solicitor of this district, and others made speeches. A joint discussion had been asked by the Populists, which was refused. The Populists put up a stand near the Court House, and Mr. Massey, a candidate for the leg slature, commenced to introduce Mr. Teague, who was to make the principal speech. Abell, who was the leader of the Redshirts, assisted by others, pulled Mr. Massey off the stand, and he was dragged across the court house square, being kicked and beaten as he was dragged, and told to leave town. Several Populists were beaten, told to leave town, and some cut with knives. Mr. Teague tried to speak, but Mr. Abell told him he could not do so, and the Red Shirts proceeded to pull down the stand. Solicitor Pou's clerk, F. H. Brooks, was among the leaders of the red shirts. A deputy sheriff, in four feet, did not try to prevent this, and said he could do nothing. Mr. Teague left with Mr. Parker and others, as it was useless to contend with the mob. Threats were made to pull down the Courier office, but this was prevented by terminated citizens.

Another mob later in the day assembled to make an attack on the Courier office, but hearing that an appeal had been made to the Governor for troops, the attack was abandoned."

The sheriff of Johnston county wired the Governor that he was master of the situation, and that peace and order was restored in the county, just as the Governor's Guard was starting from Raleigh on a special train. We are informed that the Democratic sheriff assured Mr. Massey, the candidate for the legislature, that no other speakers in the county would be interfered with. In spite of the assurance of the sheriff, on the next day, Wednesday, at Selma, Mr. Massey was dragged from the speaker's stand, kicked and beaten by a mob of red shirts.

On Tuesday Mr. Teague left Smithfield to fill his appointment at Dunn on Wednesday. Solicitor Pou and his gang of lawless red shirts got on the train and followed him. He was insulted all the way on the train by this mob. He went to a hotel in Dunn that night, and went up to his room. A little after midnight he was awakened by an armed mob, who had broken into his room, and stood over his bed with drawn pistols. They forced him to at the point of their weapons to get up and dress, and go down stairs, get into a buggy and leave the county. They also forced him to take money out of his own pocket and turn over five dollars for what they said would be to cover the expense of the trip.

This lawless outrage is so infamous that we forbear to comment upon the above facts, but leave the Christian, lawabiding people of the State to pass their own verdict.

stephen-sanders-1900-08.A1:
TWO SHOT TO DEATH
AND A THIRD PROBABLY FATALLY WOUNDED IN SCREVEN.
NEGROES KILLED WHITE MEN.
POSSE WENT FOR NEGROES AND WADE WAS WOUNDED.
Herrington and Mears, White, Shot Down by Negroes in the Northern Part of Screven County—Many Negroes Live in That Section—Sheriff Thompson, With Strong Backing, Is Pursuing the Murderers—White People Are Wrought Up.
Is Pursuing the Murderers—White People Are Wrought Up.

Sylvania, Ga., Aug. 12.—Last night about 9 o'clock, R. F. Herrington and Milton Mears, two white men, were driving in a buggy in the northern part of this (Screven) county. They met two negroes named Alexander. In passing the buggy wheels collided. Words ensued, and the negroes drew pistols and shot the white men to death.

Capt. Jesse T. Wade, living near, organized a party and went to capture the negroes. As he reached their house, he received three rapid shots, which are likely to prove fatal. One wound is in the head and one in the groin. He is in a serious condition.

The negroes—what number is not known—are quartered on the plantations bordering on the Savannah river swamps. It is claimed they are planning to resist arrest, and their number is being increased.

In the section where the tragedy occurred there are only about twenty-five white families and a hundred negroes. Sheriff Thompson has just left Sylvania with a well-armed posse to capture the negroes. There may be a serious engagement later, and developments are eagerly expected.

Capt. Wade, the wounded man, is a brother of the late ex-Senator U. P. Wade.

The Latest Report.

8 p. m.—Later—Parties have just come into town and will procure coffins for the dead men, Herrington and Mears. They report that Capt. Wade's condition is hopeful, though his recovery is in doubt. The sheriff's posse has not been heard from yet, but the young men who bring this information have no traces whatever of the negroes. They have fled.

Everything is quiet as far as far as the negroes are concerned, but the white people are wrought up up over the killing of two of their fellow citizens in cold blood, and the wounding of Capt. Wade of the Scree-ven Troops.
stephen-sanders-1900-08.A4:
NEGROES KILL TWO WHITE MEN.
RACE FEUD BREAKS OUT IN GEORGIA—
SHERIFF IN PURSUIT.
Sylvania, Ga., Aug. 12.—Last night R. F. Harrington and Milton Means, white, were driving home in their buggy. On the road they met two negroes named Alexander in a buggy. The wheels of the vehicles came in collision. A quarrel ensued, when the negroes drew pistols and shot Harrington and Means dead. The news quickly spread, and Captain Jesse L. Wade, brother of Senator U. C. Wade, organized a posse to capture the murderers.

As the posse approached the house of the Alexanders a number of shots in rapid succession were fired into it. Captain Wade fell, mortally wounded. The posse withdrew and went for Sheriff Thompson. The Sheriff with a reinforced posse is now in pursuit. In the section where the tragedy occurred the black population considerably outnumbers the white, and the information is that the colored neighbors of the Alexanders will assist them in resisting the Sheriff.
stephen-sanders-1900-08.A7:
KILLED BY NEGROES.
Two White Men Shot to Death and One Wounded.
SAVANNAH, Aug. 13. — A telegram from Sylvania, the county seat of Screvin County, telling of the killing of two white men and the wounding of another, says:

“Nine negroes were brought in this morning and lodged in jail. They are thought to have been connected with the murder of Fillmore Herrington and Milton Mears, who were shot to death on Saturday night by a mob of negroes. Other negroes who are believed to have been implicated in the shooting have crossed the Savannah River and have fled into South Carolina. The killing of Herrington and Mears was a deliberate murder. Herrington had a difficulty with a negro Saturday evening whose names was Sanders, and who told Herrington he would kill him before morning.

“Upon the advice of friends Herrington swore out a peace warrant for the negro and placed it in the hands of Constable Milton Mears. Capt. Jesse T. Wade went along with Herrington and Mears, fearing there might be trouble. When they approached the house of Jesse Sanders, father of the man who had the difficulty with Herrington in the evening, Captain Wade hailed and asked where the man wanted was. The reply was that he was there, but that he would not surrender.

“At that moment about forty shots were
"At that moment about forty shots were fired in rapid succession by negroes who were hiding in ambush near the place and the three white men fell to the ground. Herrington and Mears were killed and Captain Wade was wounded in three places, but he managed to get away and the chance for his recovery is good.

"Captain Wade is a brother of ex-State Senator U. P. Wade and is highly esteemed. He is captain of the Screvin Troop of the First Georgia Regiment of cavalry. The captain says his escape was miraculous, as he was satisfied that at least forty guns were turned loose on his party at the same time. Mears' pockets were searched and everything about his person was taken, including about $5 in money and a silver watch. A private reward of $300 has been offered and the officers think that the murderers will soon be captured.

"In the mean time the people are much wrought up, but no talk of lynching has yet been indulged in."
stephen-sanders-1900-08.A12:
TELLLS OF THE CRIME
CAPT. WADE DESCRIBES THE KILLING IN SCREVEN COUNTY.
SAYS HIS STORY IS CORRECT.
HE IS IN A HOSPITAL IN AUGUSTA FOR TREATMENT.
The Trouble Began When the White Men Met the Negro in the Road. Three Went to Make the Arrest on a Peace Warrant—Fired Upon From a Plum Thicket—Herrington and Mears Were Killed and Capt. Wade Was Wounded.

Augusta, Aug. 17.—Capt. Jesse T. Wade, who was shot a week ago in Screven county and brought to the hospital in this city, gave out to-day what he says is the only correct story of the shooting.

He says at the outset there was no race war, and nothing like it. He says two white men, R. F. Herrington and George Daniels, in a buggy, met a negro, named Stephen Sanders, in another buggy on a narrow road and the negro insolently demanded them to turn out of his way.

Herrington hit Sanders with his whip, and the negro jumped out of his buggy and ran. The mule the negro was driving was about to run off, but one of the white men caught the bridle and called to the negro to come back and get his team. As the negro drove off, after getting back into his buggy, he cursed Herrington for striking him with his whip, and said:

"I'll kill you to-night."

When the white men got to town they reported the incident to Capt. Wade, and he advised legal proceedings and had a peace warrant taken out by Herrington against the negro. About 8:30 o'clock Herrington and Daniels, with Capt. Wade and Milton Mears, in two buggles, drove out to the home of Jesse Sanders, the father of Stephen, to serve the peace warrant. When they arrived at the house, the moonlight was bright as day, and Wade Herrington and Mears advanced to the house, while Daniels remained to hold the mules.

Shot From a Thicket.

While the white men on the outside were talking with the old negro on the inside of the house and telling him to give up his son and he would not be hurt, a volley was fired from a plum thicket, a short distance to one side of the house. Capt. Wade was shot in the groin, the arm and the head, and when he rallied from the shock so as to look about him, Mears was nowhere to be seen and Herrington was running wildly a hundred yards distant. The mule attached to the buggy in which Daniels was sitting became frightened at the shooting and dashed off with him, but as he gained control of the animal he drove back and helped Wade into the buggy. The other two men were not in sight, and as there was no more shoot, ing, it is supposed the negroes ran after firing the volley.

The next morning a posse returned to the place and found the dead bodies of Herrington and Mears, the former having run several hundred yards before he fell.

That is the whole story, says Capt. Wade, except that several of the negroes were apprehended in South Carolina, and, when arrested, they implicated several more who have also been arrested. "In my opinion," says Capt. Wade, "there will be no lynching, but the law will take its course. There is no race war in Screven."

stephen-sanders-1900-08.A15:
SIX MURDERERS IN JAIL.
SCREVEN COUNTY ASSASSINS IN CUS-TODY OF SHERIFF SWEENY.
Half of the Band of Negroes Who Shot and Killed Milton Mears and Fillmore Herrington Brought to Savannah by Sheriff Thompson of Screven County—Double Possibility of a Jail Delivery or a Lynching the Reason for Their Removal Here—All of the Six Have Freely Confessed Their Part in the Crime. Six Others Are Still at Liberty.

Six members of the band of black assassins who shot and killed Fillmore Herrington and Milton Mears, two white men, in the northern part of Screven county, on the night of Aug. 11, were brought to Savannah and lodged in jail last night.

The negroes are Cleveland Herrington, Andrew Davis, Samuel Balden, Richard Sanders, William Hudson and Arnold Augustus. They were brought to Savannah by Sheriff W. B. Thompson, of Screven county, and Special Deputies S. C. Jenkins and L. B. Thompson. The reason for bringing the men to the city lay in the double possibility of a lynching, on the part of the outraged friends of the two who were so brutally murdered, and a jail-delivery, on the part of the relatives and allies of the murderers themselves.

The double homicide in Screven county is fresh in the public mind. On Saturday night, Aug. 11, Herrington and Mears went to the home of Jesse Sanders, a negro living in the country some distance from Sylvania, for the purpose of arresting one of his sons, with whom Herrington had had a difficulty on the afternoon of the same day. They were accompanied by Capt. Jesse T. Wade, a prominent citizen of that section of the state.

As they approached Sanders' house they were fired upon by a party of negroes concealed in a thicket. Herrington and Mears were killed and Capt. Wade so seriously wounded that it was with great difficulty he effected an escape.

The next morning an armed mob gathered and began a search for the negroes, and at the same time Sheriff Thompson organized a posse and started for the scene, with the double purpose of arresting the guilty parties and protecting them from the vengeance of the mob. Indignation ran high and it was only by the exercise of diplomacy, mingled with some small show of force, that the sheriff was enabled to save the lives of the three negroes who were then arrested. Since that day three others have been quietly taken into custody, making the six that have been brought to Savannah.

Everyone of them has confessed his participation in the crime, making a statement that was as full as it was voluntary and free. Their statements and the known facts in the possession of the officers implicate six other negroes in the crime, these six being supposed to be now in hiding in some of the swamps that line the Savannah river. According to the story told by the men arrested and in jail, a negro named Matthew McKinney was the arch conspirator, the ruling spirit in the deadly assault that was made on Herrington and Mears. McKinney is one of those who have made their escape, but Sheriff Thompson believes it will not be a great while before he too, is under arrest.

McKinney is said to be a gambler and desperado of the worst type, whose presence in the neighborhood has been a continual source of uneasiness and annoyance and even of danger. He aroused, by every art of the demagogue, the evil passions of the men of his race and kept them in an excited state which needed only an occasion to develop into an armed outbreak.

The negroes in jail give no real reason for their participation in the murder of Herrington and Mears, other than that they were induced to join in the felonious assault by the influence of McKinney. They confess that both white men had been uniformly kind to the members of their race and acknowledge having received many favors at their hands. Not a circumstance in evidence, not a sentence in their own statements, shows the homicide to have been other than a cold-blooded, wanton and cruel murder, equally without reason and excuse.

Since the men have been confined in the jail at Sylvania the sheriff has had it closely guarded, in the constant fear that there would be an attempt at either a jail delivery or a lynching. It is his firm opinion that the only thing that has kept the negroes he brought to Savannah alive is the fact that there were as many more at liberty. Public sentiment and indignation is at fever heat and had all the men been in custody and confined in the Sylvania jail its strong walls and the guard would have been alike unavailing to protect them from the vengeance of the mob. It was generally believed that the members of the band still at liberty would soon be apprehended. This accomplished, the friends of the men killed would have been able to make a clean sweep.

The fear of this induced the County Commissioners to direct the sheriff to bring his prisoners to Savannah. It was with a sigh of relief that they entered the jail here, knowing that they would be punished by the slow process of the law, rather than the swift and terrible methods of an outraged community.

The negroes of the better class in Screven county are anxious that the law be permitted to take its course. They have made frequent appeals to Sheriff Thompson for the protection of the men arrested and this protection he has, of course, promised and given. The preachers and other leaders of the race do not seem to cherish any hope that the fate of the men arrested will be other than death, but they think the effect will be better if this fate be brought about in the execution of the mandate of the law than if it be the work of a mob.

REWARDS FOR NEGROES.
Gov. Candler Offers Them in the Screven County Murder Case.
Atlanta, Aug. 29.—Gov. Candler this morning offered rewards for Jesse Alexander, Stephen Alexander, Bob Johnson, Matthew McKinney, Aaron Johnson and Peter Frederick, the negroes who caused the trouble in Screven county on the night of Aug. 11, when R. F. Herrington and Milton Mears were killed and Capt. J. T. Wade was dangerously wounded. The sum of $150 has been offered for the first arrest and $100 for each subsequent arrest.
